package.title: Babies Have No Bony Kneecaps (Until Age 3) 🦵
package.description:
Why are babies born without bony kneecaps? A baby's kneecap starts as soft cartilage and only begins turning to bone between about ages 3 and 6, fusing into one solid kneecap by the early teens.

Sources:
https://www.healthline.com/health/do-babies-have-kneecaps
https://radiopaedia.org/articles/24732

package.pinned_comment: Be honest: did you know you were born without bony kneecaps? 🦵
package.script: Your kneecaps were soft until you were about three. Babies don't have bony kneecaps at all. Each knee has a soft disc of cartilage instead, the same bendy stuff in the tip of your nose. So why start soft? First, there's birth itself. A hard kneecap would make that tight squeeze riskier. Then comes crawling. Knees hit the floor again and again, and soft cartilage handles that better than bone. Then somewhere between ages three and six, tiny islands of bone pop up inside the cartilage. They grow, they spread, and by your early teens they've fused into one solid kneecap. And honestly, it's kind of a weird bone. It's the biggest bone in your body that grows right inside a tendon. That's why a toddler's knees are still so squishy. So be honest. Did you know you were born without kneecaps?
key_facts: Babies are born with a kneecap made of cartilage, not bone (Healthline)
Patella ossification centers appear between about 3 and 6 years (Radiopaedia; Healthline says 2-6)
Several pieces harden and fuse into one bone by about age 10-12 / puberty
A rigid kneecap could make birth harder; cartilage handles crawling and learning to walk better (Healthline)
The patella is the largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon (Radiopaedia)

package.title: Your Liver Can Regrow 2/3 of Itself in Weeks
package.description:
Your liver is your biggest internal organ and does more than 500 jobs: it filters your blood, turns toxic ammonia into urea, makes bile to digest fat, stores glycogen, vitamins and iron, and builds clotting proteins. We paint how the liver works, why poop is brown, and how a liver can grow back after up to two thirds is removed, which is what makes living liver donors possible.

Sources:
https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/conditions-and-diseases/liver-anatomy-and-functions
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/21481-liver

package.pinned_comment: Your liver can lose two thirds of itself and grow back in weeks. Which of its jobs surprised you most: the filter, the bile factory, the pantry, or the regrowing?
package.script:
You could lose two thirds of your liver, and it would actually grow back.
In a few weeks, it's almost back to full size.
No other organ inside you can pull that off.
And while it's doing that, it's still running more than five hundred jobs.
So what is this thing, and how does it do it all?
Let's paint it out, one job at a time.
Chapter one. The biggest organ inside you.
Tuck your hand under your right ribs.
That's roughly where your liver sits.
It's a soft, reddish-brown wedge about the size of a football,
and it weighs around one and a half kilos.
That makes it your biggest internal organ.
And it's always full of blood, about a pint at any moment.
Most of that blood comes straight from your gut,
through one big pipe called the portal vein.
So everything you eat and drink passes through your liver first,
before it reaches the rest of your body.
Chapter two. The filter.
Think of your liver as a security checkpoint.
Inside, it's built from millions of tiny cells called hepatocytes,
lined up in rows like the pages of a book.
Blood seeps slowly between those rows,
and the cells grab anything that shouldn't be there.
Old medicines, leftover chemicals, and alcohol all get broken down here.
Your muscles also make a waste called ammonia,
which is toxic if it builds up.
Your liver turns it into urea,
a much safer waste that your kidneys flush out.
Chapter three. The bile factory.
Your liver also makes bile, a greenish-yellow juice,
up to about a litre of it every day.
Bile works a lot like dish soap.
It breaks big blobs of fat into tiny droplets,
so your gut can actually digest them.
Between meals, the bile waits in a little pouch called the gallbladder.
And here's a weird one.
Bile carries leftovers from old red blood cells,
and that's what turns your poop brown.
Chapter four. The pantry.
After a meal, your liver packs extra sugar away
as a starch called glycogen.
Then, between meals or while you sleep,
it turns that glycogen back into sugar,
so your brain never runs out of fuel.
It also keeps a stash of vitamin A, vitamin D,
vitamin B twelve, and iron, for later.
And it builds proteins your blood needs,
including the ones that make a cut stop bleeding.
Chapter five. The comeback organ.
Now back to that superpower.
Doctors can remove up to two thirds of a healthy liver,
and the rest starts growing right away.
The cells that are left simply divide,
and the liver can get back most of its size in a few weeks.
That's why living donors are possible.
A healthy adult gives part of their liver to someone who needs it,
and both pieces grow into full-size livers.
And scientists are still working out exactly how it knows when to stop.
So the next time you eat a meal,
remember the quiet organ under your ribs,
filtering, storing, building, and regrowing,
more than five hundred jobs, all at once.
Next time, what really happens if you swallow chewing gum?
Does it actually stay inside you for seven years?
key_facts: The liver is the largest internal (solid) organ, about 1.5 kg / 3 lb (Cleveland Clinic)
It performs more than 500 functions (Johns Hopkins Medicine)
It holds about a pint (~13%) of the body's blood at any moment; most of its blood arrives via the portal vein from the gut (Johns Hopkins)
Liver makes bile (roughly up to a litre a day), stored in the gallbladder; bilirubin from old red blood cells gives stool its brown colour
It converts ammonia to urea, stores glycogen, vitamins A, D, B12 and iron, and makes clotting proteins (Johns Hopkins)
Up to two thirds of a healthy liver can be removed; it can regenerate in as little as a few weeks, sometimes several months; in living donation both parts grow back to full size (Cleveland Clinic)

Ice cream gives you a 30-second headache,
but your brain never freezes.

but it gets mixed up,

package.title: Swallowed Gum Doesn't Stay 7 Years. So Where Does It Go?
package.description:
What really happens if you swallow chewing gum? Your body can't digest gum base, but it doesn't need to: swallowed gum moves through your stomach and intestines like corn skins and seeds and usually leaves within a few days, not seven years. Sources:

package.script:
Swallowed gum never stays in you for seven years.
It's actually gone in a few days.
So where did the seven-year story come from?
And what actually happens to gum inside you?
Let's follow one swallowed piece, all the way through.
Chapter one. The seven-year myth.
Almost everyone hears it as a kid.
Swallow your gum, and it sits in your stomach for seven years.
Nobody really knows who started it.
But there's a grain of truth hiding inside.
Your body can't digest gum. Not properly.
It just doesn't need to.
Chapter two. What gum is made of.
People have chewed gummy stuff for thousands of years.
In Denmark, scientists found a lump of chewed birch tar
about five thousand seven hundred years old.
It still held the chewer's DNA, and her tooth marks.
Far away, the Maya chewed chicle,
a milky sap tapped from the sapodilla tree.
In the eighteen seventies, an inventor named Thomas Adams
started selling chicle as chewing gum in America.
Today most gum starts with a gum base,
made of rubbery, food-grade polymers.
Then sweetener, softeners and flavour get mixed in.
Chapter three. Why you can't digest it.
Digestion is mostly chemistry.
Your spit, stomach and gut make enzymes,
tiny molecular scissors that snip food into pieces.
One kind cuts starch, one cuts protein, and one cuts fat.
The sugar and flavour in gum dissolve away while you chew.
But the gum base is made of long, tangled chains
that none of those scissors can cut.
Even your stomach acid barely touches it.
So the rubbery part stays rubbery, the whole way through.
And honestly, that's fine.
Your body handles stuff it can't digest every single day.
Chapter four. The journey out.
Once you swallow, the gum slides down your food pipe in seconds.
In your stomach, strong muscle walls churn it with your lunch.
Then it squeezes through a little gate at the bottom,
into your small intestine,
a tube roughly six metres long, all folded up.
Waves of muscle push it along, like toothpaste in a tube.
And between meals, your gut runs a cleanup cycle.
Every ninety minutes to two hours or so,
a strong wave sweeps the leftovers onward.
Scientists nicknamed it the housekeeper.
The gum rides along with corn skins, seeds and fibre,
through the large intestine,
and out with everything else, usually within a few days.
Chapter five. When it can go wrong.
So one swallowed piece is no big deal.
But doctors have reported rare cases in young kids
who swallowed gum every day, piece after piece.
The gum clumped together, sometimes with coins or seeds,
into a sticky ball that got stuck.
Those cases are rare, and they took a lot of gum.
So the best place for gum is still the bin, not your belly.
The seven-year myth is wrong,
but it's wrong in an interesting way.
Your body can't break gum down.
It simply moves it along, and shows it the door.
Next time, why are sloths so slow?
And how does being slow keep them alive?

Gum base (food-grade polymers, resins, elastomers) resists digestive enzymes; sweeteners and flavours dissolve or are absorbed
A ~5,700-year-old chewed birch-pitch 'gum' from Syltholm, Denmark yielded a full human genome and oral microbes (Scientific American / Nature Communications 2019)
The Maya and Aztecs chewed chicle, sap from the sapodilla tree (Manilkara zapota); Thomas Adams began selling chicle chewing gum in New York in the early 1870s
Between meals the migrating motor complex sweeps the stomach and small intestine roughly every 90-120 minutes ('housekeeper' wave)
The small intestine is roughly 6 m (about 20 ft) long
Rare gum bezoars have been reported in children who habitually swallowed large amounts of gum, sometimes with coins or seeds (Milov et al., Pediatrics 1998)

00:00:38,500 --> 00:00:40,930

14
00:00:41,290 --> 00:00:44,690
People have chewed gummy stuff for thousands of years.

15
00:00:45,170 --> 00:00:48,800
In Denmark, scientists found a lump of chewed birch tar

16
00:00:49,190 --> 00:00:51,620
about five thousand seven hundred years old.

17
00:00:52,030 --> 00:00:55,420
It still held the chewer's DNA, and her tooth marks.

18
00:00:55,780 --> 00:00:57,930
Far away, the Maya chewed chicle,

19
00:00:58,280 --> 00:01:00,820
a milky sap tapped from the sapodilla tree.

20
00:01:01,270 --> 00:01:04,890
In the eighteen seventies, an inventor named Thomas Adams

21
00:01:05,150 --> 00:01:08,700
started selling chicle as chewing gum in America.

22
00:01:09,080 --> 00:01:11,450
Today most gum starts with a gum base,

23
00:01:11,800 --> 00:01:14,210
made of rubbery, food-grade polymers.

24
00:01:14,570 --> 00:01:17,880
Then sweetener, softeners and flavour get mixed in.

25
00:01:18,330 --> 00:01:20,880
Chapter three. Why you can't digest it.

26
00:01:21,280 --> 00:01:23,860
Digestion is mostly chemistry.

27
00:01:24,230 --> 00:01:27,030
Your spit, stomach and gut make enzymes,

28
00:01:27,420 --> 00:01:30,870
tiny molecular scissors that snip food into pieces.

29
00:01:31,220 --> 00:01:35,410
One kind cuts starch, one cuts protein, and one cuts fat.

30
00:01:35,780 --> 00:01:39,720
The sugar and flavour in gum dissolve away while you chew.

31
00:01:40,080 --> 00:01:43,340
But the gum base is made of long, tangled chains

32
00:01:43,740 --> 00:01:45,630
that none of those scissors can cut.

33
00:01:46,090 --> 00:01:48,960
Even your stomach acid barely touches it.

34
00:01:49,420 --> 00:01:52,810
So the rubbery part stays rubbery, the whole way through.

35
00:01:53,170 --> 00:01:55,060
And honestly, that's fine.

36
00:01:55,370 --> 00:01:59,280
Your body handles stuff it can't digest every single day.

37
00:01:59,630 --> 00:02:01,790
Chapter four. The journey out.

38
00:02:02,190 --> 00:02:06,260
Once you swallow, the gum slides down your food pipe in seconds.

39
00:02:06,690 --> 00:02:10,450
In your stomach, strong muscle walls churn it with your lunch.

40
00:02:10,900 --> 00:02:13,360
Then it squeezes through a little gate at the bottom,

41
00:02:13,770 --> 00:02:15,320
into your small intestine,

42
00:02:15,670 --> 00:02:18,740
a tube roughly six metres long, all folded up.

43
00:02:19,210 --> 00:02:23,030
Waves of muscle push it along, like toothpaste in a tube.

44
00:02:23,410 --> 00:02:26,890
And between meals, your gut runs a cleanup cycle.

45
00:02:27,330 --> 00:02:29,510
Every ninety minutes to two hours or so,

46
00:02:29,920 --> 00:02:32,850
a strong wave sweeps the leftovers onward.

47
00:02:33,240 --> 00:02:35,830
Scientists nicknamed it the housekeeper.

48
00:02:36,270 --> 00:02:40,000
The gum rides along with corn skins, seeds and fibre,

49
00:02:40,420 --> 00:02:41,900
through the large intestine,

50
00:02:42,270 --> 00:02:45,720
and out with everything else, usually within a few days.

51
00:02:46,060 --> 00:02:48,430
Chapter five. When it can go wrong.

52
00:02:48,830 --> 00:02:51,900
So one swallowed piece is no big deal.

53
00:02:52,360 --> 00:02:55,420
But doctors have reported rare cases in young kids

54
00:02:55,720 --> 00:02:59,120
who swallowed gum every day, piece after piece.

55
00:02:59,550 --> 00:03:03,220
The gum clumped together, sometimes with coins or seeds,

56
00:03:03,570 --> 00:03:05,600
into a sticky ball that got stuck.

57
00:03:06,030 --> 00:03:09,410
Those cases are rare, and they took a lot of gum.

58
00:03:09,770 --> 00:03:13,400
So the best place for gum is still the bin, not your belly.

59
00:03:13,760 --> 00:03:15,450
The seven-year myth is wrong,

60
00:03:15,800 --> 00:03:17,750
but it's wrong in an interesting way.

61
00:03:18,210 --> 00:03:20,430
Your body can't break gum down.

62
00:03:20,800 --> 00:03:23,750
It simply moves it along, and shows it the door.

63
00:03:24,220 --> 00:03:26,590
Next time, why are sloths so slow?

64
00:03:27,070 --> 00:03:29,570
And how does being slow keep them alive?

topic.title: Why do your teeth chatter when you're cold?

package.title: Why Teeth Chatter: Shivering Makes 5x the Heat 🥶
package.description:
Why do your teeth chatter when you're cold? Your brain's hypothalamus makes your muscles shiver to generate heat, and your small, light, hinged jaw rattles so your teeth click together.

Sources:
https://www.scienceabc.com/humans/why-do-your-teeth-chatter-when-youre-cold.html

package.pinned_comment: When you're freezing, what chatters first: your teeth or your knees? 🥶
package.script: Your chattering teeth mean your brain is burning fuel before you freeze. When your skin senses cold, a spot deep in your brain called the hypothalamus hits the panic button. It can't just crank up a thermostat, so it makes your muscles shiver. Tiny fast squeezes, over and over, and every squeeze burns fuel and leaks heat. At full blast, shivering can make about five times the heat your body makes at rest. Your jaw muscles join in too. But your jaw is small and light, and it hangs on a hinge, so every twitch swings it. Top teeth smack bottom teeth. Click, click, click. Your legs and back are shivering too, they're just too heavy to rattle. And honestly, that's kind of genius. Your body turns its own muscles into a furnace. So be honest. When you're freezing, what chatters first, your teeth or your knees?
key_facts: Shivering is involuntary rapid muscle contraction triggered by the brain (hypothalamus) to make heat (PopSci)
Peak shivering measured at 4.9x resting metabolism; ~5x reported (Eur J Appl Physiol 2001, PubMed 11394237)
Chattering happens because face and jaw muscles shiver too, banging the teeth together (ScienceABC)
Jaw is a light, hinged bone, so its shivering is visible/audible while bigger muscles' shivering isn't (explanatory)

topic.title: Why don't vultures get sick from eating rotten meat?

package.title: Why Vultures Eat Rot: Stomach Acid at pH 1 🦅
package.description:
Why don't vultures get sick from eating rotten meat? Their stomach acid sits close to pH 1 and kills most germs, and the tough gut bacteria that survive, Clostridia and Fusobacteria, help digest the carcass.

Sources:
https://insider.si.edu/2014/11/vultures-remarkably-tolerant-to-deadly-bacteria-study-reveals
https://www.nature.com/news/microbes-help-vultures-eat-rotting-meat-1.16345

package.pinned_comment: Which grosses you out more: the rotten meat, or the gut full of flesh-eating bacteria? 🦅
package.script: Vultures eat rotten meat that would kill you, and never get sick. Why? A carcass can be crawling with germs like anthrax, and the vulture keeps eating. First, the stomach. Vulture stomach acid sits close to pH 1, nearly as strong as battery acid. Most germs die right there. In one study of fifty vultures, scientists found five hundred twenty-eight kinds of bacteria on their faces, but only seventy-six made it to the gut. And the ones that survive? Tough, meat-eating microbes called Clostridia and Fusobacteria, germs that make most other animals sick. In a vulture, they're on the team, helping break down the meal. By cleaning up carcasses, vultures stop those germs from spreading. So be honest. Which grosses you out more, the rotten meat, or the gut full of flesh-eating bacteria?

topic.title: The Mantis Shrimp Paradox: how does a thumb-sized shrimp punch hard enough to crack glass?

package.title: How a Tiny Shrimp Cracks Glass in 0.003 Seconds 🦐
package.description:
How does a mantis shrimp the size of your thumb punch hard enough to crack aquarium glass? Muscles squeeze a saddle-shaped spring in its arm, a latch holds it, and when the latch lets go the club fires at about 80 km/h in under three thousandths of a second, so fast the water boils into bubbles that collapse and hit its prey a second time.

Sources:

https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/the-mantis-shrimp-has-the-worlds-fastest-punch

package.pinned_comment: If a mantis shrimp can crack glass, what would YOU keep it in? 🦐
package.script:
A shrimp the size of your thumb
punches at 80 kilometers an hour,
hard enough to crack glass. How?
Meet the mantis shrimp.
It doesn't pinch with claws.
It swings a club folded under its head.
And the trick isn't muscle.
Big muscles squeeze a spring
shaped like a saddle,
kind of like a Pringles chip.
A tiny latch holds it locked.
Then, click, the latch lets go.
The club fires in under three thousandths of a second.
So fast the water in front of it boils into bubbles.
When those bubbles collapse,
they slam the shell a second time,
with a flash of light and heat.
One punch, two hits.
Snail shells don't stand a chance.
And when the club wears down?
It just molts and grows a fresh one.
So if it can crack glass,
what would you keep it in?

package.script:
Mint never cools your mouth, not even one degree.
So why does it feel freezing?
It's a trick, and your brain falls for it.
Your mouth is packed with tiny cold alarms.
At body temperature they stay quiet,
and they only start ringing below about twenty-six degrees Celsius.
That's around seventy-nine Fahrenheit.
But mint carries a molecule called menthol,
and it fits that alarm like a key.
Now the alarm rings at a cozy thirty-seven degrees,
and shouts to your brain: freezing!
Yet your mouth hasn't cooled down one bit.
That's why a sip of water after mint gum
feels like you just drank a glacier.
The alarms are already primed,
so even cool water feels icy.
And honestly, it's the same trick chili plays,
just on the heat alarm instead.
Be honest, did you think mint was actually cold?

Chili's capsaicin plays the same trick on the heat receptor TRPV1

package.pinned_comment: Armour like the pill bug or speed like the sow bug: which one would you pick, and why?
package.script:
Pill bugs roll into balls,
but you've never seen the real reason why.
First, they aren't bugs at all.
They're crustaceans,
cousins of crabs, shrimp and lobsters.
Count the legs. Fourteen, not six.
Their back is a row of hard, overlapping plates.
But their belly is soft,
with legs and tiny gills.
Yep, gills.
They breathe like their sea cousins,
so they have to stay damp.
Now poke one, or shake the ground.
It tucks its head, folds its tail,
and the plates lock into a perfect armoured ball.
A hungry ant just finds a smooth shell
with nothing soft to grab.
And inside, the ball traps moisture,
so those gills don't dry out.
Their cousins, sow bugs, can't roll up.
They just run for it.
So, armour or speed?
Which one would you pick?

They have seven pairs of legs (14 legs)
They breathe with gill-like structures and need humid conditions; they can't breathe if it's too dry
Rolling up (conglobation) when threatened or when the ground vibrates puts the tough plates outward and shields the soft belly and legs
Rolling up also helps them hold in moisture and avoid drying out
Sow bugs, close relatives, cannot roll into a ball

topic.title: Why are sloths so slow? (and why it keeps them alive)

package.title: Why Sloths Take Up to 30 Days to Digest a Meal 🦥
package.description:
Why are sloths so slow? A leafy diet gives them almost no energy, so sloths run on the lowest metabolism of any mammal, digest a single meal for weeks, and stay alive by barely moving, which hides them from harpy eagles and big cats. We draw the whole survival plan on a whiteboard: the slowest stomach, the weekly trip down to poop, the moths and green algae living in sloth fur, and the organs anchored to their ribs.

Sources:
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3906947
https://a-z-animals.com/animals/sloth/what-sloths-eat-and-how-it-explains-their-famous-slowness/

package.pinned_comment: Before this video, did you think sloths were just lazy? And which fact surprised you most: the month-long meal, the weekly poop trip, or the algae garden?
package.script:
Being slow is the reason sloths are still alive,
and you'd never guess why.
Sloths aren't lazy.
Their slowness is a survival plan,
and every part of their body is built around it.
Let's draw it out.
Chapter one. A diet with almost no fuel.
Sloths live high up
in the rainforests of Central and South America.
And they mostly eat leaves.
Leaves are tough, full of fibre,
and some are even a bit toxic.
They give a sloth very little energy.
So a sloth runs its body
like a phone on low battery.
Its metabolism is less than half
of what you'd expect for an animal its size.
And it has about thirty percent less muscle
than other mammals its size.
Chapter two. The slowest stomach.
A sloth's stomach has several chambers,
full of microbes that slowly break leaves down.
A full stomach can make up a big chunk of its weight.
Some scientists think one leafy meal
can take up to a month to pass all the way through.
That's the slowest digestion of any mammal.
And to save even more energy,
a sloth lets its body temperature drift with the weather.
On chilly mornings, it sunbathes to warm up,
like a lizard with fur.
Chapter three. The weekly trip.
Here's the strangest part.
About once a week,
a three-toed sloth climbs all the way down
to the ground, just to poop.
It digs a little hole, does its business,
and climbs back up.
That trip burns a lot of energy,
and it's the most dangerous thing a sloth ever does.
So why bother?
Scientists think it helps
a tiny moth that lives in its fur.
The moths lay eggs in the dung.
The babies grow up, fly into the trees,
and find a new sloth to live on.
Chapter four. A garden on its back.
Sloth hair has tiny cracks that soak up rainwater.
Green algae grow inside them,
so a sloth can look a little green.
The moths seem to feed that algae,
and the sloth may lick some off as a snack.
In one study,
a sloth carried about a hundred and twenty grams of algae.
Chapter five. Slow means invisible.
A sloth's biggest enemies
are harpy eagles and big cats.
Many of these hunters spot prey by its movement.
A sloth barely moves,
and it can look green and mossy,
so it blends right into the leaves.
To an eagle scanning the treetops,
a sloth just looks like part of the tree.
Even its body helps it hang around.
Its organs are anchored to its ribs,
so they don't squash its lungs when it hangs upside down.
And here's a bonus.
In water,
sloths are surprisingly good swimmers.
They paddle with those long arms,
often faster than they can crawl on land.
So sloths aren't failing at being fast.
They're winning at being slow.
In a jungle full of hunters,
saving energy and staying unseen beats speed every time.
Next time, how does your heart
beat about a hundred thousand times a day?
key_facts: Three-toed sloths have an exceedingly low metabolic rate, less than half that expected for their body mass, and the slowest digestion of any mammal (Pauli et al. 2014, Proc R Soc B)
Sloths have the lowest basal metabolic rate of any mammal; muscle is about 25-30% of body mass vs 40-45% in most mammals (A-Z Animals; Sloth Conservation Foundation: ~30% less muscle)
Some sources say a leaf can take up to ~30 days to pass through a sloth's gut; the exact rate is debated
Sloths' body temperature varies with the environment and they bask to warm up
About once a week three-toed sloths descend to defecate at the base of the tree; the trip costs energy and most adult deaths are predation (Pauli et al. 2014)

Sloth moths (Cryptoses) lay eggs in sloth dung; larvae develop there and adults fly up to colonise sloths; moths are linked to more algae (Trichophilus) in the cracked hair, which sloths may eat; algal biomass averaged ~125 g (Pauli et al. 2014)
Harpy eagles are the primary aerial predator; algae may camouflage sloths from above (Live Science)
Fibrinous adhesions anchor sloths' abdominal organs to the lower ribs so they don't press on the lungs when hanging upside down (Cliffe et al. 2014, Biology Letters; National Geographic)
Sloths are capable swimmers, reported to move faster in water than on the ground (Sloth Conservation Foundation)

package.script:
Ostriches never bury their heads in sand,
but you've seen it happen. Why?
Blame a Roman writer, Pliny the Elder,
nearly two thousand years ago.
He wrote that ostriches hide their heads in bushes
and think nobody can see them.
Here's what's really going on.
Ostriches dig a shallow hole in the ground
and lay their giant eggs inside.
Several times a day, mom and dad dip their heads down
and roll each egg with their beak.
From far away, the head vanishes.
And if danger's close and they can't get away,
they flop flat, neck stretched along the dirt,

package.script:
Salt makes your dessert sweeter.
You've probably never noticed why.
Bakers sneak it into cookies,
caramel and chocolate.

Trick number one.
Most foods hide a little bitterness,

like muting the loudest guy in the room.

Trick number two.
Scientists found your sweet taste cells have a tiny sugar door
called S G L T one.

topic.title: Your Heart Explained in Simple Words: how it beats about 100,000 times a day

package.title: Who Tells Your Heart to Beat 100,000 Times a Day?
package.description:
How does your heart work? Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day without your brain telling it to: it is two pumps in one, four chambers, four one-way valves that make the lub-dub sound, and its own built-in pacemaker, the sinoatrial node, that fires an electrical spark about once a second. We paint the whole heart open in watercolour, from the blood's trip to your lungs and back to the AV node's tiny pause, then add up the numbers: around 2,000 gallons of blood a day and more than two and a half billion beats in a long life.

Sources:

https://www.cedars-sinai.org/health-topics/anatomy-and-function-of-the-electrical-system
https://med.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Anatomy_and_Physiology/Anatomy_and_Physiology_(Boundless)/17%3A_Cardiovascular_System%3A_The_Heart/17.4%3A_Physiology_of_the_Heart/17.4C%3A_Heart_Sounds

package.script: Your heart beats 100,000 times a day, and nobody tells it to. It's only about the size of your fist, it weighs less than a pound, and it hasn't taken a day off since before you were born. So how does one lump of muscle keep that up? Let's paint it open. Part one. Two pumps in one. Your heart isn't really one pump. It's two pumps, side by side, sharing one wall. Each side has two rooms. A small atrium on top, and a big, strong ventricle below. Four chambers in total. The right side gets tired blood back from your body, low on oxygen. It squeezes that blood a short hop over to your lungs. There it drops off carbon dioxide and picks up fresh oxygen. Then the bright red blood flows back into the left side. And the left side has the big job. It pushes blood all the way to your toes and back. That's why its bottom wall is two to three times thicker. It's the bodybuilder of the family. Part two. The lub-dub. Put your ear on someone's chest. Lub, dub. Lub, dub. You might think that's the muscle squeezing. It's actually the sound of doors slamming. Your heart has four valves, little flaps that only open one way. When the ventricles squeeze, the valves between the top and bottom rooms snap shut. That's the lub. A moment later the ventricles relax, and the valves at the exits snap shut, so nothing flows backward. That's the dub. One-way doors. That's the whole trick that keeps blood moving forward. Part three. The built-in spark. Now the really weird part. Your heart doesn't wait for your brain to tell it to beat. It has its own pacemaker, a tiny patch of cells called the sinoatrial node. About once a second it fires an electrical spark. The spark races across the top chambers, and they squeeze first. Then it hits a second checkpoint, the AV node, which holds the signal for about a tenth of a second, so the top rooms finish emptying before the big bottom rooms fire. Your brain can speed it up or slow it down, when you run, or when you sleep. But the beat itself starts inside the heart. That's why a donor heart can keep beating for a little while even after it's been taken out of the body. Part four. The numbers. A hundred thousand beats a day adds up fast. Every day your heart pumps around 2,000 gallons of blood. That's roughly a full bathtub every single hour. One blood cell can loop your whole body in about a minute. And over a long life, your heart will beat more than two and a half billion times. All without a single break. Part five. Feel it yourself. Every beat is a tiny relay race. Spark, squeeze, lub, dub. Lungs, body, and back again. Put two fingers on the inside of your wrist. That little tap is your left ventricle, pushing blood all the way down to your hand. Next time, we'll follow your breath. How do your lungs pull in air over 20,000 times a day?

The heart is roughly fist-sized and weighs under a pound
Four chambers: two atria on top, two ventricles below; the right side pumps to the lungs, the left side to the body
The left ventricle wall is about two to three times thicker than the right
Lub = the AV (tricuspid and mitral) valves closing; dub = the aortic and pulmonary valves closing
The sinoatrial node is the heart's natural pacemaker; the AV node delays the signal about a tenth of a second
The heart pumps about 2,000 gallons of blood a day
A heart beats more than 2.5 billion times over a long life

topic.title: Why do penguins waddle?

package.title: Why Do Penguins Waddle? The 80% Trick 🐧
package.description:
Why do penguins waddle? Their short legs make walking expensive, but the side-to-side waddle works like a pendulum, letting emperor penguins win back up to 80% of the energy in each stride, more than the roughly 65% people recover when walking.

package.pinned_comment: Be honest: before this, did you think penguins waddle because they're clumsy, or did you guess it was on purpose?
package.script:
Penguins waddle on purpose,
and you'd never guess the 80 percent reason.
It looks clumsy, but that wobble is a trick.
The problem is their legs.
They're super short,
so every step is quick and tiny,
and quick steps burn fuel fast.
Back in the seventies, scientists found
walking penguins use about twice the energy
of other animals their weight.
Then in 2000, researchers walked emperor penguins
across a plate that measures every push.
The waddle turned out to be a pendulum.
Each lean to the side lifts the body a little,
then the swing back turns that lift into the next step.
That way penguins win back up to 80 percent of the energy in each stride.
You only get back about 65.
Without the wobble,
their muscles would have to make up the difference.
So next time a penguin waddles past,
is it clumsy, or kind of brilliant?

topic.title: Why don't Antarctic fish freeze solid?

package.title: How Fish Survive −1.9°C Water Without Freezing 🧊
package.description:
Why don't Antarctic fish freeze solid in seawater colder than their blood's normal freezing point? Icefish and their cousins make antifreeze proteins that bind to tiny ice crystals and stop them growing, and the gene for them evolved from a digestive enzyme gene.

package.script: Your goldfish would freeze solid in this minus 1.9 degree water, so how does this fish survive? The sea around Antarctica stays liquid because salt lowers its freezing point. But normal fish blood freezes at about minus 0.7. So a regular fish would turn into a fishsicle. The trick is hiding in its blood. Antarctic icefish and their cousins make antifreeze proteins. When a tiny ice crystal sneaks inside, the proteins grab onto its surface and stop it from growing. The crystal stays too small to do harm. Scientists even found ice in their spleens, all year round. And the wildest part? The antifreeze gene evolved from a gene for a digestive enzyme. Evolution recycled a gut gene into a winter coat. So would you trade your blood for antifreeze and swim in minus 1.9 degree water?

topic.title: Why don't ducks' feet freeze on ice?

package.title: Why Don't Duck Feet Freeze at 0°C? 🦆
package.description:
Why don't ducks' feet freeze on ice? A countercurrent heat exchange in their legs lets warm arterial blood hand its heat to cold blood returning from the feet, so mallards lose only about 5% of their body heat through their feet.

Sources:
https://askanaturalist.com/why-don%E2%80%99t-ducks%E2%80%99-feet-freeze/
https://www.wwt.org.uk/discover-wetlands/blog/why-dont-birds-feet-freeze-and-other-amazing-avian-adaptations

package.pinned_comment: Would you swap feet with a duck for one winter? Yes or no way? 🦆
package.script: Ducks stand barefoot on ice for hours, and their feet never freeze. Yours would. Why? A duck's body runs hot, around 41 degrees. If that warm blood rushed into its feet, the ice would suck the heat right out. So inside each leg, there's a trick. The artery carrying warm blood down runs tight against the veins coming back up. As they pass, the warm blood hands its heat to the cold blood heading home. Scientists call it countercurrent heat exchange. So the feet only get blood that's barely warm, just enough to dodge frostbite, and the heat goes back into the body. In one study, mallards at freezing lost only about 5 percent of their body heat through their feet. And duck feet are mostly bone and tendon, with hardly any soft tissue to freeze. Pretty genius, right? So would you swap feet with a duck, just for one winter?

Mallards lost only about 5% of their body heat through their feet at 0 C (askanaturalist, citing study)
Bird legs and feet are relatively free of soft tissue; foot muscles sit higher in the leg and work via long tendons (askanaturalist)
Bird body temperature is about 106 F / ~41 C (Audubon via Forest Preserve District of Will County)

package.title: 1 Starfish Arm Grows 4 New Arms. How? ⭐
package.description:
How do starfish regrow a lost arm? Sea stars can drop an arm on purpose to escape a crab, seal the wound, and rebuild the arm from the tip back over a few months to more than a year, and Linckia sea stars can grow a whole new body from a single arm.

package.pinned_comment: If one arm grows into a whole new starfish, which one is the real starfish: the original or the new one?
package.script:
You can't regrow a finger,
but one starfish arm can grow
four new arms and a whole body.
When a crab grabs one, it can drop the arm on purpose.
A muscle at the base squeezes, and the arm lets go.
Then the wound seals itself shut,
and skin creeps over it in about two days.
Muscle cells turn back into simpler cells
and crawl toward the stump.
The first part to grow back?
A tiny tube foot at the tip.
It works like a signal tower,
telling everything behind it where to grow.
Tube feet, little bones and muscle fill in, one by one.
The whole arm takes a few months to over a year.
And in Linckia sea stars,
one arm alone can grow a brand new body.
So if one arm can make a whole starfish,
which one is the real starfish?

The terminal tube foot is the first structure to regrow and acts as a signalling centre; other tube feet, ossicles and muscle follow

tags: how do geckos stick to walls
package.pinned_comment: Would you trade your feet for gecko feet if it meant size 114 shoes? 🦎
package.script:
What if your feet could hold 290 pounds with no glue?
A gecko's feet can, at least in theory.
Its toes are covered in tiny hairs,
about six and a half million on one gecko.
And every hair splits into hundreds of even tinier tips.
Those tips get so close to the wall
that the molecules themselves pull together.
It's called the van der Waals force.
One hair is weak,
but millions together are mighty.
To let go, a gecko just peels its toes up,
like tape.
Now scale that up to you.
You'd need sticky pads on forty percent of your body,
about eighty percent of your front!
And your shoes? US size one hundred fourteen.
That's why geckos are about the biggest animals that can do this.
So would you trade your feet for gecko feet?

package.script:
Touch a spider web and you'll stick.
So how does the spider touch its glue 1,000 times a web?
First, not every thread is sticky.
The spokes and the frame are dry silk.
Only the spiral is beaded with tiny glue drops,
so the spider walks on the spokes.
But while building,
it still bumps the glue hundreds to thousands of times.
The real secret is in its legs.
They're covered in tiny branching hairs.
A glue drop only touches a few hair tips,
and slides right off.
The legs also have a non-stick coating.
When scientists washed it off,
the legs suddenly stuck way harder.
And the spider moves carefully,
peeling each foot away at just the right angle.
Dry spokes, hairy feet, and a built-in non-stick layer.
Honestly, that's kind of genius.
If a spider walked onto another spider's web,
would it get stuck?

package.pinned_comment: Do your freckles fade in winter, or do they stick around all year?
package.script: You were born with zero freckles. Not a single one. They usually start showing up around age two. Then some kids get a few, while others end up with hundreds. So why do some people get way more freckles than others? First, what is a freckle, really? Your skin gets its color from a pigment called melanin. It's made by special cells called melanocytes, tucked deep in the bottom layer of your skin. Each one pumps out tiny packets of pigment, and hands them to the skin cells around it. Here's the surprise. A freckle doesn't have extra pigment cells. It has about the same number as the skin next to it. Those cells are just working way harder, making a lot more melanin in one tiny spot. Most freckles are smaller than three millimeters. And they show up most on fair skin, which has less melanin to begin with. So what makes those cells work overtime? Sunlight. When ultraviolet light hits your skin, it switches your melanocytes into high gear. Melanin is your body's sunshade. It soaks up UV light before it can damage your DNA. In most skin, that extra melanin spreads out evenly, and you get a tan. But in freckly skin, it piles up in little patches. That's why freckles darken every summer, and fade, or even disappear, in winter. And it's why babies, who've barely seen the sun, don't have any yet. But two kids can play in the same sun, and only one ends up covered in freckles. That's where your genes come in. The big one is a gene called MC1R. Think of it as a switch on every melanocyte. When it works normally, the cell makes eumelanin, a dark brown pigment that's great at blocking sun. But scientists have found more than 80 versions of MC1R. And some of them are ancient. One may date back around 80,000 years. Some of them flip the switch toward pheomelanin instead, a reddish yellow pigment that protects much less. Those same versions are behind red hair. Most redheads carry two of them, and almost all carry at least one. That's why red hair and freckles so often go together. Still, one copy doesn't guarantee freckles. Some people without these versions freckle anyway, because lots of other genes play a part too. Now, not every brown spot is a freckle. Doctors call real freckles ephelides. Real freckles come and go with the seasons, and many fade as you get older. Sun spots, or solar lentigines, are different. They're larger, they show up in middle age, after years of sun, and they stay put all winter long. Under a microscope, sun spots really do have extra pigment cells. So what do freckles tell you? Freckly skin usually makes less of that protective brown melanin, so it burns more easily. That's why skin doctors tell freckly people, to be extra careful with sunscreen. So freckles aren't random dots. They're tiny patches of sunshade, switched on extra hard, mostly thanks to one tiny gene. Next up, how do your lungs breathe, more than 20,000 times a day?

It's made by special cells called melanocytes,

10
00:00:22,080 --> 00:00:24,270
tucked deep in the bottom layer of your skin.

11
00:00:24,620 --> 00:00:27,080
Each one pumps out tiny packets of pigment,

12
00:00:27,480 --> 00:00:29,460
and hands them to the skin cells around it.

13
00:00:29,810 --> 00:00:30,940
Here's the surprise.

14
00:00:31,270 --> 00:00:33,550
A freckle doesn't have extra pigment cells.

15
00:00:34,000 --> 00:00:36,500
It has about the same number as the skin next to it.

16
00:00:36,920 --> 00:00:38,940
Those cells are just working way harder,

17
00:00:39,350 --> 00:00:42,080
making a lot more melanin in one tiny spot.

18
00:00:42,490 --> 00:00:45,000
Most freckles are smaller than three millimeters.

19
00:00:45,420 --> 00:00:47,240
And they show up most on fair skin,

20
00:00:47,600 --> 00:00:49,340
which has less melanin to begin with.

21
00:00:49,770 --> 00:00:51,890
So what makes those cells work overtime?

22
00:00:52,360 --> 00:00:53,040
Sunlight.

23
00:00:53,380 --> 00:00:55,300
When ultraviolet light hits your skin,

24
00:00:55,710 --> 00:00:57,970
it switches your melanocytes into high gear.

25
00:00:58,320 --> 00:01:00,180
Melanin is your body's sunshade.

26
00:01:00,530 --> 00:01:03,670
It soaks up UV light before it can damage your DNA.

27
00:01:04,070 --> 00:01:07,240
In most skin, that extra melanin spreads out evenly,

28
00:01:07,570 --> 00:01:08,460
and you get a tan.

29
00:01:08,910 --> 00:01:11,720
But in freckly skin, it piles up in little patches.

30
00:01:12,160 --> 00:01:14,100
That's why freckles darken every summer,

31
00:01:14,450 --> 00:01:16,980
and fade, or even disappear, in winter.

32
00:01:17,430 --> 00:01:19,700
And it's why babies, who've barely seen the sun,

33
00:01:19,930 --> 00:01:20,810
don't have any yet.

34
00:01:21,260 --> 00:01:23,250
But two kids can play in the same sun,

35
00:01:23,600 --> 00:01:25,810
and only one ends up covered in freckles.

36
00:01:26,180 --> 00:01:27,520
That's where your genes come in.

37
00:01:27,980 --> 00:01:30,360
The big one is a gene called MC1R.

38
00:01:30,750 --> 00:01:33,060
Think of it as a switch on every melanocyte.

39
00:01:33,510 --> 00:01:34,500
When it works normally,

40
00:01:34,810 --> 00:01:36,060
the cell makes eumelanin,

41
00:01:36,450 --> 00:01:39,200
a dark brown pigment that's great at blocking sun.

42
00:01:39,620 --> 00:01:43,130
But scientists have found more than 80 versions of MC1R.

43
00:01:43,480 --> 00:01:44,890
And some of them are ancient.

44
00:01:45,310 --> 00:01:47,830
One may date back around 80,000 years.

45
00:01:48,270 --> 00:01:51,070
Some of them flip the switch toward pheomelanin instead,

46
00:01:51,540 --> 00:01:54,270
a reddish yellow pigment that protects much less.

47
00:01:54,690 --> 00:01:56,950
Those same versions are behind red hair.

48
00:01:57,310 --> 00:01:58,940
Most redheads carry two of them,

49
00:01:59,280 --> 00:02:00,940
and almost all carry at least one.

50
00:02:01,330 --> 00:02:04,100
That's why red hair and freckles so often go together.

51
00:02:04,530 --> 00:02:07,060
Still, one copy doesn't guarantee freckles.

52
00:02:07,530 --> 00:02:10,170
Some people without these versions freckle anyway,

53
00:02:10,600 --> 00:02:12,830
because lots of other genes play a part too.

54
00:02:13,290 --> 00:02:15,590
Now, not every brown spot is a freckle.

55
00:02:16,070 --> 00:02:18,230
Doctors call real freckles ephelides.

56
00:02:18,650 --> 00:02:20,910
Real freckles come and go with the seasons,

57
00:02:21,270 --> 00:02:22,920
and many fade as you get older.

58
00:02:23,360 --> 00:02:26,180
Sun spots, or solar lentigines, are different.

59
00:02:26,590 --> 00:02:28,900
They're larger, they show up in middle age,

60
00:02:29,010 --> 00:02:30,020
after years of sun,

61
00:02:30,370 --> 00:02:32,040
and they stay put all winter long.

62
00:02:32,490 --> 00:02:36,450
Under a microscope, sun spots really do have extra pigment cells.

63
00:02:36,840 --> 00:02:38,310
So what do freckles tell you?

64
00:02:38,860 --> 00:02:42,460
Freckly skin usually makes less of that protective brown melanin,

65
00:02:42,840 --> 00:02:44,310
so it burns more easily.

66
00:02:44,750 --> 00:02:47,030
That's why skin doctors tell freckly people,

67
00:02:47,360 --> 00:02:49,280
to be extra careful with sunscreen.

68
00:02:49,690 --> 00:02:51,530
So freckles aren't random dots.

69
00:02:51,880 --> 00:02:53,530
They're tiny patches of sunshade,

70
00:02:53,870 --> 00:02:55,170
switched on extra hard,

71
00:02:55,470 --> 00:02:57,440
mostly thanks to one tiny gene.

72
00:02:57,870 --> 00:02:59,690
Next up, how do your lungs breathe,

73
00:03:00,050 --> 00:03:01,760
more than 20,000 times a day?

package.pinned_comment: If you could keep growing forever but every growth spurt got riskier, would you take the deal? 🦞
package.script:
Lobsters never stop growing.
So why don't you see 40-pound ones?
First, a lobster lives inside hard armor.
To get bigger, it climbs right out of it.
The old shell splits open across the back
and the lobster wriggles free,
claws, legs and all.
Then it gulps seawater and swells up
before the new soft shell hardens.
A young lobster molts about 25 times
in its first few years.
And deep in its cells
an enzyme called telomerase
keeps repairing their DNA,
so the cells keep dividing.
That's how one lobster in Nova Scotia
grew to 20 kilograms.
That's 44 pounds!
But here's the catch.
Every molt costs more energy.
Some old lobsters die of exhaustion mid-molt.
Others just stop molting,
stuck in a worn-out shell.
So would you want to keep growing forever?
key_facts: Lobsters have indeterminate growth: they keep molting their whole lives
They split the shell, pull free, swell with seawater and the new soft shell hardens
Young lobsters molt about 25 times in their first 5-7 years
Telomerase stays active in lobster tissues, helping cells keep dividing
Heaviest lobster on record: 20.15 kg (44 lb 6 oz), Nova Scotia, 1977 (Guinness)
Molting costs more energy with size; some old lobsters die mid-molt and others stop molting and get shell disease

topic.title: How does a snake swallow something bigger than its head without choking?

package.title: 3 Tricks Snakes Use to Swallow Meals Wider Than Their Heads
package.description:
How do snakes swallow prey wider than their own heads without choking? Their lower jaw halves are joined by a stretchy ligament and walk the meal in one side at a time, the windpipe opening pushes forward so they keep breathing, and their ribs only attach to the spine so the body stretches.

package.pinned_comment: What's the biggest thing you think a snake could swallow? 🐍
package.script: Snakes never choke on meals wider than their own heads. Your jaw could never. So how? First, a myth. Snakes don't unhinge their jaws. The two halves of the lower jaw aren't fused at the chin. A stretchy ligament joins them, so they spread wide apart. Then each side moves on its own. Left grips, right slides forward, then left again. The snake basically walks its head over its meal. But with a mouth that full, how does it breathe? Its windpipe opening sits low in the mouth, and it can push forward and off to the side, like a built-in snorkel. And its ribs only attach to the spine, so the whole body stretches around the meal. King snakes can even swallow other snakes as long as themselves. So what's the biggest thing you think a snake could swallow?
key_facts: Snake jaws do not dislocate; the two lower jaw halves are not fused and are joined by elastic tissue (Live Science; NHM)
The two sides of the jaw move independently, ratcheting over the prey (king snake 'pterygoid walk', Live Science)
The glottis can move to allow breathing while swallowing large prey (WikiVet)
Snake ribs attach only to the spine (NHM)

You'd never miss a snack again
with a chameleon's tongue.
But talking? Ruined.
A chameleon's tongue can stretch
over twice its body length.

bunched up inside your mouth.
And it's fast.

and the sticky tip lands first.

so a bug can't pull free.

package.description:

Sources:
https://www.nature.com/articles/429363a
https://www.sciencenews.org/article/red-sweat-hippo-skin-oozes-antibiotic-sunscreen

package.pinned_comment: If your sweat could be any color, which one would you pick? 🎨
package.script:
Hippos sweat bright red, but not blood.
How do they never get sunburned when you would?
Hippos spend their days soaking in African rivers,
but they often haul out onto sunny banks,
and their skin has a super thin outer layer
that dries out fast.
So it oozes a thick, oily goo.
At first it's clear.
Then, within minutes,
it turns bright red,
and later, brown.
People call it blood sweat,
but it's not blood,
and it's not really sweat either.
Scientists found two pigments inside it,
one red and one orange.
Both soak up ultraviolet light,
like built-in sunscreen.
And the red one slows down germs,
so scrapes from hippo fights stay cleaner.
Sunscreen and germ fighter,
in one gooey coat.
So if your sweat could be any color,
which one would you pick?
key_facts: Hippos secrete a viscous fluid from skin glands (not true sweat, not blood) that starts colorless and turns red, then brown, within minutes
It contains a red pigment (hipposudoric acid) and an orange one (norhipposudoric acid), identified by Saikawa et al., Nature 2004
Both pigments absorb ultraviolet light, acting as a natural sunscreen
The red pigment inhibits the growth of some bacteria
Hippo skin has a thin outer layer and loses water quickly in the air; hippos spend much of the day in water

package.title: How Do Your Lungs Breathe 20,000 Times a Day?
package.description:
How do your lungs work? Your lungs can't breathe on their own: the diaphragm pulls air down a branching airway tree into about 480 million alveoli, where oxygen swaps into your blood and carbon dioxide comes out.

Sources:
https://www.livescience.com/52250-lung.html
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulmonary_alveolus
https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/lung-and-airway-disorders/biology-of-the-lungs-and-airways/control-of-breathing

package.pinned_comment: Before this video, did you think your lungs did the pulling, or the diaphragm? 🫁
package.script:
Your lungs can't breathe on their own,
yet you breathe more than 20,000 times a day,
without ever thinking about it.
So what's really pulling the air in?
And what happens to it once it's inside?
Let's follow one breath, all the way in.
First, the engine.
And it isn't your lungs.
It's a muscle underneath them, called the diaphragm,
a dome shaped like an upside-down bowl.
When you breathe in, it tightens and pulls down flat.
Your ribs swing up and out at the same time.
Your chest gets bigger,
so the air pressure inside drops,
and outside air rushes in to fill the space.
Your lungs just stretch along, like balloons in a box.
Breathing out at rest is even easier.
The diaphragm relaxes,
and your stretchy lungs spring back like a rubber band,
pushing the air out.
Each calm breath moves about half a liter.
Over a whole day, that's roughly 10,000 liters of air.
Now let's follow that air inside.
It goes down your windpipe, the trachea,
which splits into two tubes, one for each lung.
Then those tubes split again, and again,
about 23 times,
into thinner and thinner branches.
Doctors call it the bronchial tree,
because it looks like a tree growing upside down.
Lay every tube end to end,
and by one estimate, they'd stretch about 2,400 kilometers.
The tubes are lined with sticky mucus and tiny hairs called cilia.
They trap dust and germs,
and sweep them back up toward your throat,
where you swallow them without noticing.
And your lungs aren't twins.
The right one has three sections, called lobes.
The left one has only two,
because it leaves room for your heart.
Now here's where the magic happens.
At the end of every tiny branch,
there's a bunch of air sacs, like grapes.
They're called alveoli.
And you've got around 480 million of them.
Each one is wrapped in a net of tiny blood vessels.
The wall between the air and your blood,
is about 200 times thinner than a sheet of paper.
So oxygen just slips across, into your blood.
At the same time, carbon dioxide, your body's waste gas,
slips the other way, into the air sac,
ready to be breathed out.
Spread all those sacs out flat,
and they'd cover about 70 square meters.
That's roughly a badminton court,
folded up inside your chest.
So who's in charge of all this?
Not you, most of the time.
A spot in your brainstem runs breathing on autopilot.
And here's the surprise.
It mostly isn't watching your oxygen.
It's watching carbon dioxide.
When CO2 builds up in your blood,
your brainstem tells the diaphragm to breathe faster.
That burning need to breathe when you hold your breath?
That's mostly carbon dioxide piling up, not oxygen running out.
In fact, the air you breathe out still has about 16 percent oxygen,
compared to 21 percent going in.
So your lungs aren't really pumps.
They're a giant, folded-up trading floor,
where air and blood swap gases,
over 20,000 times a day, every day of your life.
Next up, why can some animals see colors,
we can't even imagine?

Quiet exhalation is mostly passive elastic recoil
A resting breath is about 0.5 L; roughly 20,000 breaths a day
Airways branch about 23 times (bronchial tree); one estimate puts total airway length near 2,400 km
Right lung has 3 lobes, left has 2 (cardiac notch)
About 480 million alveoli, about 70 square meters of surface
The blood-air barrier is well under a micrometer thick
The brainstem drives breathing mainly from CO2 levels
Exhaled air still holds about 16% oxygen vs about 21% inhaled

package.script: This shark drowns if you make it stop swimming. Wait, a fish that drowns? Sharks pull oxygen out of water as it flows over their gills. A nurse shark can lie still on the sea floor and pump water in with its cheeks. But a great white can't do that. Neither can makos or whale sharks. They use ram ventilation. They swim with their mouths slightly open so water gets pushed over their gills. Stop swimming, and the water stops. No water, no oxygen. So even while it's resting, a great white keeps cruising at about two kilometers an hour. That's slower than you walk! Most sharks can take a break, though. So which shark would you rather be? The one that naps on the sand, or the one that can never stop?

package.title: Why Don't Woodpeckers Get Headaches at 20 Hits/Sec? 🐦
package.description:
Woodpeckers hammer trees up to 20 times a second, so why don't they get concussions? High-speed video from a 2022 study shows a woodpecker's head isn't a shock absorber at all: it's a stiff hammer, and its tiny brain is what keeps it safe.

https://www.sci.news/biology/woodpecker-pecking-11004.html
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/woodpecker-skulls-dont-absorb-shock-like-previously-thought-180980426/

package.pinned_comment: If a woodpecker were as big as you, could it still peck? 🤔
package.script: Woodpecker pecks would concuss you. They do up to 20 a second, around 12,000 a day, and never get a headache. Why? For years, people said their skull was a shock absorber, like a built-in helmet. But in 2022, scientists filmed woodpeckers with high-speed cameras. And the head didn't cushion anything. The beak and the brain stopped together, like one stiff hammer. Which honestly makes sense. Nobody builds a hammer with a sponge inside. It would waste every swing. So the real secret is size. A woodpecker's brain is hundreds of times smaller than yours, and tiny brains can take much bigger jolts. That jolt that would knock you out? For them, it's well below the danger line. They'd have to hit twice as fast to get hurt. So if a woodpecker were as big as you, could it still peck?
key_facts: Woodpeckers can peck up to about 20 times a second and around 12,000 times a day

The head does not absorb shock: beak and brain decelerate together, so the head acts as a stiff hammer
Each peck's deceleration exceeds the concussion threshold for humans, but small brains tolerate far bigger decelerations
Normal pecking stays well below a woodpecker's concussion threshold; they would need to hit about twice as fast to be at risk
